gloss: photogenic quality; looking good (especially on social media); visual appeal

definitions.gloss: photogenic quality; visual appeal; looking good on social media
definitions.explanation: The quality of looking attractive or eye-catching, especially in photos posted to social media. Derived from the verb {映|は}える (to look attractive). Became widespread as a buzzword associated with Instagram culture.

examples.japanese: ⟦この→この：00962_kono⟧⟦{料理|りょうり}→料理：01523_ryouri⟧⟦は→は：00079_ha⟧{映|ば}え⟦する→する：00392_suru⟧。
{映|ば}え⟦スポット→スポット：11578_supotto⟧⟦を→を：00422_wo⟧⟦{探|さが}して→探す：00493_sagasu⟧⟦カフェ→カフェ：06767_kafe⟧⟦を→を：00422_wo⟧⟦{巡|めぐ}った→巡る：03930_meguru⟧。
examples.english: We went around cafes looking for photogenic spots.

examples.japanese: ⟦{最近|さいきん}→最近：00881_saikin⟧⟦の→の：09472_no⟧⟦レストラン→レストラン：01048_resutoran⟧⟦は→は：00079_ha⟧⟦{味|あじ}→味：00826_aji⟧⟦だけでなく→〜だけでなく：18373_dakedenaku⟧{映|ば}え⟦も→も：00484_mo⟧⟦{意識|いしき}した→意識する：17974_ishikisuru⟧⟦{盛|も}り{付|つ}け→盛り付け：05754_moritsuke⟧⟦が→が：00051_ga⟧⟦{多|おお}い→多い：01127_ooi⟧。
examples.english: Restaurants these days often have presentation that is designed with visual appeal in mind, not just taste.

notes:
Short for ⟦インスタ→インスタ：28008_insuta⟧{映|ば}え (looking good on Instagram), which was selected as one of Japan's buzzwords of the year in 2017. The standalone {映|ば}え has since become a general term for photogenic or visually appealing things, used beyond just Instagram.

COMMON COLLOCATIONS:
- {映|ば}え⟦スポット→スポット：11578_supotto⟧: a photogenic spot
- {映|ば}え⟦する→する：00392_suru⟧: to be photogenic; to look good (in photos)
- {映|ば}え⟦{写真|しゃしん}→写真：00753_shashin⟧: a photo that looks great (on social media)
- ⟦インスタ→インスタ：28008_insuta⟧{映|ば}え: Instagram-worthy
- {映|ば}え⟦を→を：00422_wo⟧⟦{狙|ねら}う→狙う：00313_nerau⟧: to aim for a photogenic look

SIMILAR WORDS:
- {映|は}える: to look attractive; to stand out — the verb form; the standard dictionary reading is はえる
- フォトジェニック: photogenic — the English loanword, used more in formal or media contexts

USAGE:
The kanji {映|ば}え is a rendaku-influenced reading from {映|は}える. While some people use it self-deprecatingly or sarcastically, it remains a standard part of modern casual Japanese, especially among younger speakers.
